Base directory for this skill: /Users/ahp/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/mattpocock-skills/1.3.1/skills/engineering/code-review

Two-axis review of the diff between HEAD and a fixed point the user supplies:

  • Standards: does the code conform to this repo's documented coding standards?
  • Spec: does the code faithfully implement the originating issue / spec?

Both axes run as parallel sub-agents so they don't pollute each other's context, then this skill aggregates their findings.

The issue tracker should have been provided to you. If not, tell the user to run /setup-matt-pocock-skills.

Process

1. Pin the fixed point

Whatever the user said is the fixed point (a commit SHA, branch name, tag, main, HEAD~5, etc.). If they didn't specify one, ask for it.

Capture the diff command once: git diff <fixed-point>...HEAD (three-dot, so the comparison is against the merge-base). Also note the list of commits via git log <fixed-point>..HEAD --oneline.

Before going further, confirm the fixed point resolves (git rev-parse <fixed-point>) and the diff is non-empty. A bad ref or empty diff should fail here, not inside two parallel sub-agents.

2. Identify the spec source

Look for the originating spec, in this order:

  1. Issue references in the commit messages (#123, Closes #45, GitLab !67, etc.), fetched via the workflow in the tracker doc.
  2. A path the user passed as an argument.
  3. A spec file under docs/, specs/, or .scratch/ matching the branch name or feature.
  4. If nothing is found, ask the user where the spec is. If they say there isn't one, the Spec sub-agent will skip and report "no spec available".

3. Identify the standards sources

Search the repo for every file that documents how code should be written. When CODING_STANDARDS.md or CONTRIBUTING.md exists, it must be on the list.

On top of whatever the repo documents, the Standards axis always carries the smell baseline below: a fixed set of Fowler code smells (Refactoring, ch.3) that applies even when a repo documents nothing. Two rules bind it:

  • The repo overrides. A documented repo standard always wins; where it endorses something the baseline would flag, suppress the smell.
  • Always a judgement call. Each smell is a labelled heuristic ("possible Feature Envy"), never a hard violation. Like any standard here, skip anything tooling already enforces.

Each smell reads what it is → how to fix; match it against the diff:

  • Mysterious Name: a function, variable, or type whose name doesn't reveal what it does or holds. → rename it; if no honest name comes, the design's murky.
  • Duplicated Code: the same logic shape appears in more than one hunk or file in the change. → extract the shared shape, call it from both.
  • Feature Envy: a method that reaches into another object's data more than its own. → move the method onto the data it envies.
  • Data Clumps: the same few fields or params keep travelling together (a type wanting to be born). → bundle them into one type, pass that.
  • Primitive Obsession: a primitive or string standing in for a domain concept that deserves its own type. → give the concept its own small type.
  • Repeated Switches: the same switch/if-cascade on the same type recurs across the change. → replace with polymorphism, or one map both sites share.
  • Shotgun Surgery: one logical change forces scattered edits across many files in the diff. → gather what changes together into one module.
  • Divergent Change: one file or module is edited for several unrelated reasons. → split so each module changes for one reason.
  • Speculative Generality: abstraction, parameters, or hooks added for needs the spec doesn't have. → delete it; inline back until a real need shows.
  • Message Chains: long a.b().c().d() navigation the caller shouldn't depend on. → hide the walk behind one method on the first object.
  • Middle Man: a class or function that mostly just delegates onward. → cut it, call the real target direct.
  • Refused Bequest: a subclass or implementer that ignores or overrides most of what it inherits. → drop the inheritance, use composition.

4. Spawn both sub-agents in parallel

Issue both sub-agent calls together, in the foreground, and aggregate the reports they return.

Standards sub-agent prompt should include:

  • The full diff command and commit list.
  • The list of standards-source files you found in step 3, plus the smell baseline from step 3 pasted in full (the sub-agent has no other access to it).
  • The brief: "Report, per file/hunk where relevant, (a) every place the diff violates a documented standard: cite the standard (file + the rule); and (b) any baseline smell you spot: name it and quote the hunk. Distinguish hard violations from judgement calls: documented-standard breaches can be hard, but baseline smells are always judgement calls, and a documented repo standard overrides the baseline. Skip anything tooling enforces. Under 400 words."

Spec sub-agent prompt should include:

  • The diff command and commit list.
  • The path or fetched contents of the spec.
  • The brief: "Report: (a) requirements the spec asked for that are missing or partial; (b) behaviour in the diff that wasn't asked for (scope creep); (c) requirements that look implemented but where the implementation looks wrong. Quote the spec line for each finding. Under 400 words."

If the spec is missing, skip the Spec sub-agent and note this in the final report.

5. Aggregate

Present the two reports under ## Standards and ## Spec headings, verbatim or lightly cleaned. Do not merge or rerank findings, because the two axes are deliberately separate (see Why two axes).

End with a one-line summary: total findings per axis, and the worst issue within each axis (if any). Don't pick a single winner across axes: that's the reranking the separation exists to prevent.

Why two axes

A change can pass one axis and fail the other:

  • Code that follows every standard but implements the wrong thing → Standards pass, Spec fail.
  • Code that does exactly what the issue asked but breaks the project's conventions → Spec pass, Standards fail.

Reporting them separately stops one axis from masking the other.

1	# Watchmaker's Bench — Brief & Spike Plan
2	
3	Oct 27, 2026 · @Akash Parikh
4	
5	## Concept
6	
7	The Watchmaker's Bench lets anyone learn why a mechanical watch keeps good or bad time by diagnosing and regulating a live, simulated movement. It is the primary plan; the escapement spike below decides whether it is viable within the first 45 minutes.
8	
9	**Pitch:** a physics-driven 2D movement on a workbench, read through a timegrapher, the instrument real watchmakers use. The timegrapher shows rate (seconds per day), amplitude (degrees) and beat error (milliseconds). The reviewer adjusts the watch and watches those numbers respond.
10	
11	**Why it is non-obvious:** Bartosz Ciechanowski's *Mechanical Watch* (2022) already explains how each part works, with 3D animation. This project does not compete on that. It moves from "how does it work" to "why does it run fast, and how do I fix it" — intuition built through diagnosis, not narration.
12	
13	**Theme fit:** Theme 1, Exploration & Understanding: a simulation of a complex system that builds deep understanding. No LLM calls at runtime; Claude Code is the development story, shown through the transcripts.
14	
15	**Time:** tracked separately by Akash, under the 8-hour hard limit. No time plan is imposed on the agent; the only gate is the spike's go / no-go.
16	
17	## Experience
18	
19	A reviewer opens the link and is solving a puzzle within 30 seconds, with no data or watch knowledge needed.
20	
21	**Layout:** the movement on the left (escapement, balance, simplified gear train), the timegrapher trace and readouts on the right, controls below.
22	
23	**Watch picker:** a dropdown of movements to work on. Each entry is a parameter set for the same simulation core: beat rate, balance inertia, mainspring torque curve, tooth count, and which puzzles apply. Start with one calibre; add a second (for example an 18,000 bph vintage movement and a 28,800 bph modern one) only once the core is stable, so the picker shows the physics changing rather than only the artwork.
24	
25	**Controls:**
26	
27	- Regulator index (shortens or lengthens the effective hairspring)
28	- Mainspring state of wind (full to run down)
29	- Balance inertia (timing screws)
30	- Beat adjustment
31	- Watch position (dial up, crown down, and so on)
32	- Time speed: real time to slow motion of one beat
33	
34	**Demo mode = diagnosis puzzles.** Each puzzle loads a bundled faulty watch with a symptom and a goal:
35	
36	| Puzzle | Symptom | Hidden cause | Fix |
37	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
38	| Runs fast | Gains about 40 s/day | Regulator off-centre | Move the index toward slow |
39	| Out of beat | Uneven tick, high beat error | Hairspring stud rotated | Adjust the beat |
40	| Afternoon slump | Fine when wound, drifts by evening | Low amplitude as the mainspring runs down | Explain the trade-off; there is no single knob |
41	| Position error | Good dial up, bad crown down | Poise error | Compare positions on the trace |
42	
43	Puzzle 1 ships first; the others follow. Puzzle 3 is the teaching moment: some errors are physics, not adjustment.
44	
45	**Difficulty ladder (stretch):** puzzles are ordered from one-knob fixes (Runs fast) to multi-cause faults (Position error) to open-ended builds. Later puzzles can require background reading: each links to the relevant section of Ciechanowski's *Mechanical Watch* as the "manual", so the Bench is the lab and the blog post is the textbook. The capstone is **Make your own complication**: given the gear train's output, the user wires up a date wheel or power-reserve indicator by choosing ratios and triggers, and the Bench checks that it advances correctly. This doubles as the complication stretch item in Scope.
46	
47	## Scope
48	
49	The core is one movement, one instrument and a handful of puzzles; stretch items are added only after the core is deployed and stable.
50	
51	**Core:**
52	
53	- Swiss lever escapement, balance wheel and hairspring, drawn to stay visually correct
54	- Mainspring torque curve feeding amplitude
55	- Timegrapher: tick trace, rate, amplitude, beat error
56	- Diagnosis puzzles, starting with one
57	- Watch picker with one calibre
58	
59	**Stretch, in priority order:**
60	
61	1. More puzzles and watch positions
62	2. A second calibre in the picker, with different physics
63	3. One complication, built as the capstone puzzle (a date wheel is the cheapest; a chronograph is a second gear train and is out)
64	
65	**Out:**
66	
67	- 3D rendering; automatic winding; multiple complications
68	- Any runtime LLM or backend
69	- Mobile-first layout (it must not break on a phone, but desktop is the target)
70	
71	**Ordering rule for the agent:** core items are built and deployed before any stretch item starts. Stretch items go in the order above, each as its own branch, so an unfinished one never blocks the submission.
72	
73	## Architecture
74	
75	Simulation and rendering are strictly separate, so a bad drawing can never corrupt the physics and a renderer can be swapped without touching tested code.
76	
77	&#91;embedded content: architecture · sim core, two views, tests\]
78	
79	Controls and puzzles set parameters; the core advances state each tick; the movement view and timegrapher only read it. A watch catalog (one JSON entry per calibre) feeds the controls, so a new watch is data, not code. A complication would be a second state machine driven by the gear train's output. Stack: Vite + TypeScript + plain SVG, Vitest for the core, Playwright for render checks, static deploy.
80	
81	## Escapement spike
82	
83	The spike tests the riskiest visual — the escapement locking and releasing in sync with the balance — in a throwaway page, timeboxed to 45 minutes.
84	
85	**Setup (5 min):** a fresh repo folder `spike/`, one HTML file plus one TypeScript module, Vite dev server, Playwright installed for screenshots. Keep the spike out of the main app; it may be thrown away.
86	
87	**Steps:**
88	
89	1. **Parameterized geometry (10 min).** Ask Claude to define the escape wheel (15 teeth), pallet fork and balance from a small set of named parameters: tooth count, lift angles, lock angle, drop. Shapes must be derived from those numbers, never hand-drawn paths.
90	2. **State machine before pictures (10 min).** Model one beat as phases: lock → unlock → impulse → drop → lock. Write tests first (`/tdd`): the escape wheel advances exactly half a tooth per beat; the pallet never overlaps a tooth; the balance swings both ways.
91	3. **Render (10 min).** Draw the state as flat SVG in a technical-drawing style. The renderer reads state only; it computes nothing.
92	4. **Look and correct (10 min).** Screenshot five phases of one beat with Playwright. Have Claude compare each frame to the phase it should show, and fix what is off.
93	5. **Slow-motion check.** Play one beat at 1/20 speed and watch it yourself. Your eye is the final judge.
94	
95	**Prompt seed for step 1:**
96	
97	> Build only a Swiss lever escapement as a 2D SVG in `spike/`. All geometry must come from named parameters in one config object. Before drawing, write a pure function `escapementState(t)` that returns angles for balance, fork and wheel plus the current phase, with unit tests for the invariants in the plan. Do not build anything else.
98	
99	**Record during the spike:** the number of correction rounds, what Claude got wrong, and how you caught it. That is design-doc and video material whatever the outcome.
100	
101	## Go / no-go evaluation
102	
103	At minute 45, score the spike on five criteria; any "fail" on a must-pass criterion triggers the fallback or the pivot.
104	
105	| Criterion | Must pass? | Pass | Fail |
106	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
107	| Invariant tests | Yes | All green, no skipped tests | Tests fail or were weakened to pass |
108	| Visual correctness at 1/20 speed | Yes | No clipping; lock, impulse and drop are visible | Parts overlap or engage at the wrong moment |
109	| Convergence | Yes | Each correction round fixed more than it broke | Fixes keep reintroducing earlier bugs |
110	| Correction rounds | No | 3 or fewer | 6 or more |
111	| Readability | No | A non-expert can follow one beat | Correct but unreadable |
112	
113	**Decision:**
114	
115	- **Go:** all must-pass criteria pass. Build the full Bench.
116	- **Fallback:** tests pass but the visual fails. Keep the Bench, replace the escapement with a schematic balance wheel and a phase indicator. The timegrapher and puzzles still carry the idea. Note this as a deliberate scoping call in the design doc.
117	- **Pivot:** tests fail or the fixes are not converging. Switch to Harness Lab (see the pivot brief). The spike transcript becomes evidence of a scoping decision, which the brief explicitly rewards.
118	
119	Spend at most 15 extra minutes if the result is borderline. Past 1 hour total, decide.
120	
121	## Claude Code workflow
122	
123	The workflow is designed so the transcripts show you steering: aligning first, testing physics, verifying visuals, and rejecting wrong output.
124	
125	| Step | Tool | What it shows reviewers |
126	| --- | --- | --- |
127	| Align on the design | `/grill-with-docs` | You make the design calls; horology terms land in `GLOSSARY.md` |
128	| Check the physics | `/research` | Claims checked against primary sources before they become code |
129	| Build the sim | `/tdd` | Invariants as tests; red-green-refactor |
130	| Verify visuals | Custom `verify-render` skill | You extended the toolkit for this project's real failure mode |
131	| Review before deploy | `/code-review` | Parallel review subagents (standards + spec) |
132	
133	**The `verify-render` skill** (written by you, early): start the dev server, screenshot named states via Playwright, run numeric geometry assertions (no overlap, lock angle within tolerance), and report failures as test output. Vision alone is too weak for fine geometry; numbers make "looks wrong" actionable.
134	
135	**Judgment moments to look for and keep:** Claude asserting incorrect horology, a test weakened to pass, a render that runs but looks wrong. Correct them visibly in the transcript.
136	
137	## Physics to verify and risks
138	
139	Every physics claim below gets checked with `/research` before it becomes code; none of the numbers here are verified yet.
140	
141	**Claims to verify:**
142	
143	- Balance period from inertia and hairspring stiffness (T = 2π√(I/k)), and how the regulator changes effective length
144	- Typical beat rates (for example 18,000 or 28,800 beats per hour) and how the timegrapher derives rate and beat error from tick timing
145	- How amplitude falls as the mainspring runs down, and why low amplitude changes rate (isochronism error)
146	- How position (dial up versus crown down) produces rate differences
147	- Escapement phases and typical lift angle
148	
149	**Risks:**
150	
151	| Risk | Mitigation |
152	| --- | --- |
153	| Escapement visual never looks right | Spike first; schematic fallback |
154	| Plausible but wrong physics | `/research` before code; tests on invariants |
155	| Compared to Ciechanowski | Different goal (diagnosis); 2D technical style, not 3D |
156	| Scope creep past 6 hours | Time plan with a deployable checkpoint at 2.75 hours |
157	| Reviewer gets lost | Puzzle 1 opens by default with a one-line goal |
158	
159	**Deploy:** static Vite build on Vercel or Cloudflare Pages; no backend, no keys.

1	# Escapement spike — record
2	
3	Date: 2026-11-01. Code in `spike/` (throwaway). Run it with `cd spike && npm run dev`, then open
4	`http://localhost:5173/?speed=0.05` for one beat at 1/20 speed. `npm test` runs the invariants;
5	`npm run shots` screenshots twelve phase frames into `spike/shots/`.
6	
7	## What was built
8	
9	- `src/params.ts`: one config object. Every shape derives from it; no hand-drawn paths.
10	- `src/shapes.ts`: pure geometry. Each pallet stone is an exact region (lock arc about the fork
11	  pivot, impulse plane, back edge, top edge). The same description is used for contact and for
12	  drawing, so what is drawn is what is computed.
13	- `src/sim.ts`: `escapementState(params, t)`, pure in `t`. Balance is a sinusoid; the fork follows
14	  the impulse pin while it is in the notch; the escape wheel advances as far as the stones
15	  physically allow (bisection on penetration). Phases lock / unlock / impulse / drop are read off
16	  the contact, never scripted.
17	- `src/render.ts`: SVG from shapes only. `src/main.ts`: play, step, speed, scrub, and `?phase=`
18	  URLs for screenshots.
19	- `tests/escapement.test.ts`: ten invariants, all green, none skipped.
20	
21	## Invariants tested
22	
23	1. Half a tooth (12°) per beat, measured from any locked instant.
24	2. One tooth (24°) per full period.
25	3. Wheel never runs backward beyond 0.001°.
26	4. Wheel stationary while locked with the pin out of the notch.
27	5. Lever motion never shoves the wheel by more than 0.001°.
28	6. Balance reaches ±amplitude.
29	7. Fork stays within its bankings and rests on one whenever the pin is out of the notch.
30	8. Phase sequence per beat is exactly lock → unlock → impulse → drop → lock, on both pallets.
31	9. Pallets alternate beat by beat.
32	10. No tooth vertex is ever inside a stone (beyond the contact solver's tolerance).
33	
34	## Correction rounds (sim)
35	
36	| # | Symptom | Cause | Fix | Net effect |
37	| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
38	| 1 | Wheel creeps while locked; beats asymmetric | Locking face built radial to the wheel; the stone moves on an arc about the fork pivot, so lever motion pushed the face into the tooth | Face tangent to the pivot arc | Worse (clearing penetration by moving the wheel forward drove the tooth deeper) |
39	| 2 | Same | Guessed the stone polygon was non-convex (it was, on the exit side) | Triangle-fan decomposition | No change; wrong diagnosis |
40	| 3 | Same | Chorded arc is not invariant under rotation; forward-only clearing | Exact stone region (annular sector about pivot ∩ planes); clear in either direction | 6 → 4 failures |
41	| 4 | Entry impulse never drops | Let-off placed in polar coordinates about the pivot, scaling the rise by the body radius | Cartesian let-off | 7 failures (let-off now too shallow on one side) |
42	| 5 | Same | Let-off at a different pivot radius than the lock arc lifts at a different rate (the circular-vs-equidistant pallet trade-off) | Place the let-off by construction at the drop point | 2 failures |
43	| 6 | Exit impulse releases 0.7° of lever early | Thought the stone's back arc was in the tooth path | Added a back edge | No change (harmless, kept) |
44	| 7 | Same | Free-run speed of the wheel was below the rate at which the exit face recedes, so the sim reported a false drop | Raised free-run speed | All green |
45	
46	Seven rounds. The brief's soft criterion was three or fewer; six or more is a fail on that line.
47	No round reintroduced an earlier bug; each failure was a distinct geometric fact discovered in
48	order. Rounds 2 and 6 were wasted diagnoses.
49	
50	## Tests that were restated (not loosened), for the reviewer to judge
51	
52	- "Stationary while locked" now excludes run-to-banking: after drop the lever still travels to
53	  its banking with the tooth on the locking face, and the test originally counted that as lock.
54	- "Half a tooth per beat" is now measured lock-to-lock. Entry and exit impulses are not mirror
55	  images with circular pallets, so mid-impulse the two half-periods differ by up to a degree.
56	- "Never runs backward" allows 0.001° of numerical noise from the contact solver.
57	
58	## Render rounds
59	
60	One. First frames had the stones drawn as a sliver and a sail (outline not matching the region),
61	a lever tail poking into the wheel, and bankings in the wrong place. Second frames read correctly.
62	
63	## Horology simplifications in the spike
64	
65	- Pointed (ratchet) teeth, not club teeth. Contact is tip-only; with club teeth part of the lift
66	  is on the tooth and contact is face-on-face.
67	- Zero draw. Real locking faces are angled so the wheel pulls the lever onto its banking and
68	  recoils during unlock. Here the lever parks at the banking by construction.
69	- Fork angle is linear in balance angle while the pin is in the notch (true slider-crank omitted).
70	- No guard pin, roller crescent or safety action.
71	- Balance is a pure sinusoid: the escapement is kinematic, slaved to the balance. Rate, amplitude
72	  and beat error in the Bench would come from a separate lumped model, not from this contact sim.
73	
74	## Go / no-go scoring
75	
76	| Criterion | Must pass | Result |
77	| --- | --- | --- |
78	| Invariant tests | yes | pass (10 green, 0 skipped; three restated as above) |
79	| Visual correctness at 1/20 | yes | pass (Akash watched one beat at 1/20 on 2026-11-01: no clipping; lock, impulse and drop visible) |
80	| Convergence | yes | pass (no regressions; two wasted rounds) |
81	| Correction rounds | no | fail (7) |
82	| Readability | no | likely pass: phase label, coloured active face, contact ring |
83	
84	**Decision (2026-11-01): go.** Build the full Bench.

1	# Glossary
2	
3	Terms used in code, tests and docs. Identifiers use these words, not synonyms. Entries marked
4	*(spike)* are already encoded in `spike/`; the rest enter the vocabulary when the core is built.
5	Physics claims behind them are checked in `docs/research/`.
6	
7	## Oscillator
8	
9	- **balance** — the oscillating wheel. Its angle from rest is `balanceAngle` (degrees). *(spike)*
10	- **hairspring** — the spiral spring returning the balance to rest. Its stiffness sets the period together with balance inertia.
11	- **amplitude** — peak balance angle from rest, degrees. Healthy at full wind: roughly 250–300° dial up. *(spike, as `balanceAmplitude`)*
12	- **beat** — one half-swing of the balance, from one extreme to the other. One tick. *(spike)*
13	- **beat rate** — beats per hour (bph). 18,000 bph = 5 beats/s = 0.4 s period. *(spike)*
14	- **period** — time for a full swing (two beats). *(spike)*
15	- **regulator index** — the lever that slides the curb pins along the hairspring, changing its active length and so the rate. Marked F/S or +/−.
16	- **timing screws** — screws on the balance rim; turning them in or out changes balance inertia and so the rate.
17	- **stud** — the fixed outer anchor of the hairspring. Rotating the stud carrier changes where the balance rests relative to the fork: the **beat adjustment**.
18	- **poise** — the balance's mass balance about its axis. A **poise error** (heavy spot) changes rate in vertical positions.
19	- **isochronism** — the property of keeping the same period at any amplitude. Its absence is **isochronism error**.
20	
21	## Escapement
22	
23	- **escape wheel** — the toothed wheel the gear train drives; released one half-tooth per beat. `wheelAngle` is degrees of rotation in the direction of tooth travel. *(spike)*
24	- **tooth pitch** — 360° / tooth count. 24° for 15 teeth. *(spike)*
25	- **pallet fork** (lever) — the pivoted piece carrying two pallet stones and the notch. Its angle from centre is `forkAngle`. *(spike)*
26	- **pallet stone** (pallet) — the jewel that stops and then pushes the escape wheel. **Entry** stone meets each tooth first; **exit** stone last. *(spike)*
27	- **locking face** — the stone face a tooth rests on while the wheel is stopped. *(spike)*
28	- **impulse face** — the inclined stone face a tooth slides along, pushing the fork. *(spike)*
29	- **locking corner** — where the two faces meet. **Let-off corner** — the far end of the impulse face, where the tooth leaves. *(spike)*
30	- **lock** — the phase with the tooth at rest on a locking face. `lockAngle` is the lever rotation needed to unlock. *(spike)*
31	- **unlock** — the lever lifting a stone until the tooth tip passes the locking corner. *(spike)*
32	- **impulse** — the tooth sliding along an impulse face and pushing the fork, which pushes the balance. `liftLever` is the lever rotation it spans. *(spike)*
33	- **drop** — the escape wheel in free flight between leaving one stone and landing on the other. `drop` is the wheel rotation it spans. *(spike)*
34	- **run to banking** — the lever's remaining travel after drop until it rests on a banking pin. *(spike)*
35	- **banking** — the pins that limit lever travel; the lever rests on one between beats. *(spike)*
36	- **draw** — an angle (12–15° in practice) on the locking face so the wheel's torque pulls the lever onto its banking and recoils the wheel slightly during unlock. Zero in the drawing; its energy cost is a loss term in the oscillator model.
37	- **ratchet tooth / club tooth** — pointed teeth (English lever, all lift on the pallet) versus teeth with their own impulse face (Swiss, lift split roughly 3° tooth : 5.5° pallet). The drawing uses ratchet teeth on a Swiss in-line layout; UI copy says "lever escapement".
38	- **impulse pin** (roller jewel) — the pin on the balance that enters the fork's **notch** each beat. *(spike)*
39	- **lift angle** — the balance's travel while the impulse pin is in the notch. Timegraphers assume it (52° default) to compute amplitude. *(spike, as `liftAngle`)*
40	- **tangential geometry** — the layout rule placing the fork pivot where lines tangent to the escape wheel meet, with the stones at the tangent points. *(spike)*
41	- **circular / equidistant pallets** — two conventions for where the entry and exit lock arcs sit; the choice makes the two impulses asymmetric. The spike is circular.
42	
43	## Instrument
44	
45	- **timegrapher** — the bench instrument that listens to the ticks and reports rate, amplitude and beat error.
46	- **rate** — gain or loss in seconds per day (s/day). Positive = fast.
47	- **beat error** — the difference in milliseconds between tick-to-tock and tock-to-tick intervals. Zero means the balance rests centred.
48	- **trace** — the timegrapher's dotted plot of tick timing against beat number: slope is rate, separation of the two lines is beat error.
49	
50	## Power
51	
52	- **mainspring** — the coiled spring that stores energy. Its **torque curve** falls as it unwinds, lowering amplitude.
53	- **state of wind** — how much of the mainspring's run time remains.
54	- **gear train** — the wheels between mainspring and escape wheel; simplified in the drawing.
55	
56	## Bench
57	
58	- **calibre** — a named movement; one parameter set in the watch catalog.
59	- **position** — the watch's orientation (dial up, crown down, …) during timing.
60	- **puzzle** — a bundled faulty calibre with a symptom, a hidden cause and a completion rule.
61

# Balance period, regulator index and timing screws

Research note for The Watchmaker's Bench. Written 2026-11-01. Scope: questions (a) to (d) from the
brief's "balance period from inertia and hairspring stiffness" item. No code, no other files touched.

Legend: **[V]** verified from a primary or standard reference, **[P]** plausible, secondary source only,
**[X]** could not verify. Sign convention throughout: rate in s/day is positive when the watch gains.

## (a) Period formula and stiffness vs active length

- **[V] T = 2π·√(I/k).** Derived from τ = −kθ = Iα, giving simple harmonic motion with period
  T = 2π√(I/κ); I in kg·m², κ in N·m/rad. Wikipedia, *Balance spring*, section "Physical principles"
  (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balance_spring). Horopedia (Swiss non-profit watchmaking foundation,
  public-interest status 2023) states the same relation with the same units and names T, I and C:
  https://horopedia.org/moment-of-inertia/. Ciechanowski's *Mechanical Watch* says the rate is set by
  "the stiffness of the spring, which primarily depends on its height, thickness, and length, as well as
  the type of material" and "the moment of inertia of the object that the spring rotates"
  (https://ciechanow.ski/mechanical-watch/, section "Balance").
- **[V] k ∝ 1/L, with k = E·h·t³ / (12·L) for a flat spiral of rectangular section.** Horopedia's
  hairspring page gives "Stiffness (spring rate) of the hairspring" as a function of exactly these
  variables: C (N·mm/rad), E modulus (MPa), h height, e thickness, L length
  (https://horopedia.org/?p=69799, section 4; the formula itself is an image). The 1/12 constant is
  standard beam theory: bending stiffness E·I_section with I_section = h·t³/12, and a strip of length L
  under a uniform moment M rotates by θ = M·L/(E·I_section). Engineering spring references state it as
  M = E·b·t³·θ/(12·L) (https://calculator.academy/spiral-torsion-spring-calculator/,
...

70	    69	  const r = (d: number) => (d * Math.PI) / 180;
71	    70	  const x = s.unbalance * Math.cos(r(s.heavySpotDeg)) - s.poiseCorrection * Math.cos(r(s.poiseCorrectionDeg));

284	     1	/**
285	     2	 * Tick times of a sinusoidal balance, θ(t) = A·sin(ωt), that engages the fork whenever it
286	     3	 * crosses the notch centre. If the hairspring's rest position is offset from the notch centre
287	     4	 * by `beatOffset`, the crossings are unevenly spaced: that is beat error, and it grows as
288	     5	 * amplitude falls (the same offset is a larger fraction of a smaller swing).
289	     6	 *
290	     7	 * Each tick also carries the unlock-to-lock time the timegrapher hears: the time the balance
291	     8	 * spends inside the lift angle, which is what encodes amplitude in the sound.
292	     9	 * See docs/research/02-beat-rates-and-timegrapher.md.
293	    10	 */
294	    11	export interface Tick {
295	    12	  /** Absolute time of the tick (balance passing the notch centre), seconds. */
296	    13	  t: number;
297	    14	  /** Time from the unlock pulse to the lock pulse within this beat, seconds. */
298	    15	  liftDuration: number;
299	    16	  /** Alternates each beat. */
300	    17	  parity: 0 | 1;
301	    18	}
302	    19	
303	    20	export interface TickSource {
304	    21	  /** Actual period of the balance, seconds. */
305	    22	  period: number;
306	    23	  /** Amplitude, degrees. */
307	    24	  amplitude: number;
308	    25	  /** Notch centre's angle from the hairspring rest position, degrees. Zero = in beat. */
309	    26	  beatOffset: number;
310	    27	  /** Balance travel while engaged with the fork, degrees. */
311	    28	  liftAngle: number;
312	    29	}
313	    30	
314	    31	/** Time the balance spends crossing an angular band of `band` degrees centred on `centre`. */
315	    32	function crossingDuration(s: TickSource, centre: number, band: number): number {
316	    33	  const omega = (2 * Math.PI) / s.period;
317	    34	  const A = s.amplitude;
318	    35	  const lo = Math.max(-A, Math.min(A, centre - band / 2));
319	    36	  const hi = Math.max(-A, Math.min(A, centre + band / 2));
320	    37	  return Math.abs(Math.asin(hi / A) - Math.asin(lo / A)) / omega;
321	    38	}
322	    39	
323	    40	/** The two half-period intervals between successive crossings of the notch centre. */
324	    41	export function beatIntervals(s: TickSource): [number, number] {
325	    42	  if (Math.abs(s.beatOffset) >= s.amplitude) return [s.period, 0]; // never crosses: stopped
326	    43	  const omega = (2 * Math.PI) / s.period;
327	    44	  const phi = Math.asin(s.beatOffset / s.amplitude);
328	    45	  const d1 = (Math.PI - 2 * phi) / omega;
329	    46	  return [d1, s.period - d1];
330	    47	}
331	    48	
332	    49	/** `count` consecutive ticks starting at time `start` (which is itself a tick of parity 0). */
333	    50	export function tickTimes(s: TickSource, start: number, count: number): Tick[] {
334	    51	  const [d1, d2] = beatIntervals(s);
335	    52	  const lift = crossingDuration(s, s.beatOffset, s.liftAngle);
336	    53	  const out: Tick[] = [];
337	    54	  let t = start;
338	    55	  for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) {
339	    56	    out.push({ t, liftDuration: lift, parity: (i % 2) as 0 | 1 });
340	    57	    t += i % 2 === 0 ? d1 : d2;
341	    58	  }
342	    59	  return out;
343	    60	}
344	=== src/core/timegrapher/analyze.ts
345	     1	/**
346	     2	 * The instrument. Reads a window of ticks and reports what a bench timegrapher reports.
347	     3	 * Formulas per docs/research/02-beat-rates-and-timegrapher.md (verified against the `tg`
348	     4	 * open-source timegrapher):
349	     5	 *   rate  = (T_nominal / T_measured − 1) · 86400          (+ = fast)
350	     6	 *   beat error = |d2 − d1| / 2                             (equals trace-line separation)
351	     7	 *   amplitude = (lift / 2) / sin(π · dt / T)               (dt = unlock-to-lock time)
352	     8	 */
353	     9	import type { Tick } from "../oscillator/ticks";
354	    10	
355	    11	export interface Reading {
356	    12	  rateSecondsPerDay: number;
357	    13	  beatErrorMs: number;
358	    14	  amplitudeDeg: number;
359	    15	  /** One point per tick: beat index and the tick's offset from the nominal grid, ms. */
360	    16	  trace: { beat: number; offsetMs: number; parity: 0 | 1 }[];
361	    17	  beats: number;
362	    18	}
363	    19	
364	    20	export function analyze(ticks: Tick[], nominalPeriod: number, liftAngleDeg: number): Reading | null {
365	    21	  if (ticks.length < 4) return null;
366	    22	  const beat = nominalPeriod / 2;
367	    23	  const n = ticks.length;
368	    24	  // Measured period from first and last tick of matching parity (whole periods between them).
369	    25	  const lastSame = n - 1 - ((n - 1) % 2);
370	    26	  const periods = lastSame / 2;
371	    27	  const measuredPeriod = (ticks[lastSame].t - ticks[0].t) / periods;
372	    28	  const rateSecondsPerDay = (nominalPeriod / measuredPeriod - 1) * 86400;
373	    29	
374	    30	  let d1 = 0, d2 = 0, c1 = 0, c2 = 0;
375	    31	  for (let i = 1; i < n; i++) {
376	    32	    const d = ticks[i].t - ticks[i - 1].t;
377	    33	    if (ticks[i - 1].parity === 0) { d1 += d; c1++; } else { d2 += d; c2++; }
378	    34	  }
379	    35	  const beatErrorMs = c1 && c2 ? (Math.abs(d2 / c2 - d1 / c1) / 2) * 1000 : 0;
380	    36	
381	    37	  const dt = ticks.reduce((a, k) => a + k.liftDuration, 0) / n;
382	    38	  const amplitudeDeg = liftAngleDeg / 2 / Math.sin((Math.PI * dt) / measuredPeriod);
383	    39	
384	    40	  const trace = ticks.map((k, i) => ({ beat: i, offsetMs: (k.t - ticks[0].t - i * beat) * 1000, parity: k.parity }));
385	    41	  return { rateSecondsPerDay, beatErrorMs, amplitudeDeg, trace, beats: n };
386	    42	}

450	     1	/** Incremental tick stream: extends a window of ticks from the current watch reading. */
451	     2	import type { Tick } from "../core/oscillator/ticks";
452	     3	import { beatIntervals } from "../core/oscillator/ticks";
453	     4	import type { WatchReading } from "../core/watch";
454	     5	
455	     6	export interface TickWindow { ticks: Tick[]; nextParity: 0 | 1; nextTime: number }
456	     7	
457	     8	export const emptyWindow = (): TickWindow => ({ ticks: [], nextParity: 0, nextTime: 0 });
458	     9	
459	    10	/** Append every tick due up to `untilTime` (sim seconds), keeping at most `keep` ticks. */
460	    11	export function advanceTicks(win: TickWindow, r: WatchReading, untilTime: number, keep: number): TickWindow {
461	    12	  if (!r.running) return win;
462	    13	  const src = { period: r.period, amplitude: r.amplitudeDeg, beatOffset: r.beatOffsetDeg, liftAngle: r.liftAngle };
463	    14	  const [d1, d2] = beatIntervals(src);
464	    15	  const omega = (2 * Math.PI) / r.period;
465	    16	  const half = r.liftAngle / 2, A = r.amplitudeDeg, c = r.beatOffsetDeg;
466	    17	  const clamp = (x: number) => Math.max(-A, Math.min(A, x));
467	    18	  const lift = Math.abs(Math.asin(clamp(c + half) / A) - Math.asin(clamp(c - half) / A)) / omega;
468	    19	  const ticks = win.ticks.slice();
469	    20	  let t = win.nextTime, parity = win.nextParity;
470	    21	  let guard = 0;
471	    22	  while (t <= untilTime && guard++ < 100000) {
472	    23	    ticks.push({ t, liftDuration: lift, parity });
473	    24	    t += parity === 0 ? d1 : d2;
474	    25	    parity = parity === 0 ? 1 : 0;
475	    26	  }
476	    27	  return { ticks: ticks.length > keep ? ticks.slice(ticks.length - keep) : ticks, nextParity: parity, nextTime: t };
477	    28	}

7	**[X]** could not verify. Sign convention throughout: rate in s/day is positive when the watch gains.
8	
9	## (a) Period formula and stiffness vs active length
10	
11	- **[V] T = 2π·√(I/k).** Derived from τ = −kθ = Iα, giving simple harmonic motion with period
12	  T = 2π√(I/κ); I in kg·m², κ in N·m/rad. Wikipedia, *Balance spring*, section "Physical principles"
13	  (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balance_spring). Horopedia (Swiss non-profit watchmaking foundation,
14	  public-interest status 2023) states the same relation with the same units and names T, I and C:
15	  https://horopedia.org/moment-of-inertia/. Ciechanowski's *Mechanical Watch* says the rate is set by
16	  "the stiffness of the spring, which primarily depends on its height, thickness, and length, as well as
17	  the type of material" and "the moment of inertia of the object that the spring rotates"
18	  (https://ciechanow.ski/mechanical-watch/, section "Balance").
19	- **[V] k ∝ 1/L, with k = E·h·t³ / (12·L) for a flat spiral of rectangular section.** Horopedia's
20	  hairspring page gives "Stiffness (spring rate) of the hairspring" as a function of exactly these
21	  variables: C (N·mm/rad), E modulus (MPa), h height, e thickness, L length
22	  (https://horopedia.org/?p=69799, section 4; the formula itself is an image). The 1/12 constant is
23	  standard beam theory: bending stiffness E·I_section with I_section = h·t³/12, and a strip of length L
24	  under a uniform moment M rotates by θ = M·L/(E·I_section). Engineering spring references state it as
25	  M = E·b·t³·θ/(12·L) (https://calculator.academy/spiral-torsion-spring-calculator/,
26	  https://www.formuladen.com/en/flat-spiral-spring-controlling-torque-formula/Formula-22074).
27	  Horopedia also records the trade convention "CGS number" K = C·(length) in N·mm³/rad, i.e. the
28	  length-independent product that makes k = K/L explicit.
29	- **[P] Caveat.** The k ∝ 1/L law is first-order. A real curb-pin regulator leaves play between the
30	  pins, so effective stiffness varies a little with amplitude (Wikipedia *Balance spring*, "Regulator";
31	  SJX, https://watchesbysjx.com/2025/03/rate-regulators-mechanical-movement.html). Ignore in the core sim.
32	
33	## (b) Regulator index: fractional length change to s/day
34	
35	- **[V] Direction.** Shortening the active length stiffens the spring, raises frequency, watch gains;
36	  lengthening it makes the watch lose. Wikipedia *Balance spring* "Regulator"; Horopedia
37	  "Correction of the daily rate" (https://horopedia.org/?p=69271) states "if the active length of the
38	  hairspring decreases, the frequency increases, which results in gaining time". Moving the curb pins
39	  *away* from the stud shortens the active length (fast); toward the stud lengthens it (slow).
40	- **[V] First-order relation (derivation).** T ∝ √(I/k) and k ∝ 1/L give T ∝ √L, so
41	  ΔT/T ≈ ½·ΔL/L. Rate (s/day) = −86400·ΔT/T = **−43200·ΔL/L**. Likewise rate = −43200·ΔI/I
42	  and rate = +43200·Δk/k. One s/day corresponds to ΔL/L = 2.3×10⁻⁵.
43	- **[V] Empirical anchor.** Horopedia: "If a medium-sized wristwatch is running 10 s/day slow, the
44	  active length of the hairspring must be shortened by about 0.02 mm (approximate value for a hairspring
45	  with a length of 100 mm at the counting point and a balance of 11 mm diameter oscillating at
46	  28,800 A/h)." The formula gives 43200 × 0.02/100 = 8.6 s/day; Horopedia's "about 10" agrees within
47	  the rounding of its own example. Also gives L ≈ 100 mm as a representative hairspring length.
48	- **[P] Index angle to length.** The pins slide along the outer coil, so ΔL ≈ r_outer × Δθ(rad).
49	  For r_outer = 4–5 mm, 1° of index travel = 0.07–0.09 mm, i.e. roughly **30–40 s/day per degree**
50	  when L = 100 mm (my derivation from the Horopedia numbers, no source states it directly). Consistent
51	  with a repair-forum report that "one tenth mm of movement might change as much as 40 or 50 seconds per
52	  day" (https://watchrepairtalk.com/topic/20603-watch-regulation) and with the 1881 *Watch Adjuster's
53	  Manual* (C. E. Fritts, archive.org cihm_03260, §350) treating regulator moves of "half a minute per
54	  day, or more" as routine but isochronism-threatening.
55	
56	## (c) Typical numbers
57	
58	- **[V] Beat rates.** ETA 2824-2 family: 28,800 A/h (4 Hz, T = 0.25 s), lift angle 50°, Etachron
59	  regulator (ETA Technical Communication CT 2801-2, 18.07.2006,
60	  https://www.cousinsuk.com/PDF/categories/29_ETA2801.2-ETA2836.2.pdf; Ciechanowski: "four times per
61	  second ... 8 beats per second or 28,800 beats per hour"). Vintage: "Watches made prior to the 1970s
62	  usually had a rate of 5 beats per second (18,000 BPH)" (2.5 Hz, T = 0.4 s), Wikipedia *Balance wheel*.
63	- **[V] Balance inertia order of magnitude.** "For a frequency of 4 Hz, balance inertia of 12 mg·cm²
64	  is considered to be good, since this type of balance conventionally has a diameter of 9 to 10 mm",
65	  US patent 8,414,184 B2 (2013, contributors include Nivarox-FAR SA),
66	  https://patents.google.com/patent/US8414184B2/en. 12 mg·cm² = 1.2×10⁻⁹ kg·m².
67	- **[V by derivation] Hairspring stiffness.** k = I·(2πf)². With I = 1.2×10⁻⁹ kg·m²:
68	  4 Hz gives 7.6×10⁻⁷ N·m/rad; 2.5 Hz with the same I gives 3.0×10⁻⁷ N·m/rad. Firgelli's calculator
69	  pages quote 1.9×10⁻⁷ for a "4 Hz" 1.2×10⁻⁹ balance, which only follows if f = 2 Hz; their numbers are
70	  internally inconsistent and unsourced, so do not use them (https://www.firgelliauto.com/blogs/mechanisms/hairspring).
71	- **[P] Regulator sensitivity on real calibres.** No manufacturer figure found. Secondary sources:
72	  Etachron fine screw spans "+/-15 to 20 seconds" (https://calibercorner.com/etachron); vintage pocket
73	  watch "major marks are somewhere around one minute per day" (forum,
74	  https://www.watchprosite.com/horological-meandering/technical-question/17.1488341.14215956/);
75	  Fritts 1881, §310: "One beat in 5 minutes would (in an 18,000 train) be ... about one minute per day."
76	- **[X] 18,000 bph balance inertia.** No source gives I for a vintage calibre. Larger balances have
77	  larger I; treat any value as a design choice, not a fact.
78	- **[X] Daniels *Watchmaking* and de Carle *Practical Watch Repairing*.** archive.org copies are
79	  lending-only (HTTP 401/404 for full text); not consulted. Nothing above rests on them.
80	
81	## (d) Timing screws and rim mass
82	
83	- **[V] Sign.** Horopedia (https://horopedia.org/?p=69271, section 3): moving screw or weight mass
84	  "toward the inside of the balance, its moment of inertia is decreased and its frequency ... increases,
85	  causing the watch to run fast"; outward increases I, watch runs slow. I = m·r², so
86	  rate = −43200·ΔI/I. Opposite screws must be moved equally or the balance goes out of poise
87	  (Boley manuals below; Horopedia; Wikipedia *Balance wheel*).
88	- **[V] Magnitude, manufacturer tool manuals (Gebr. Boley).** Rolex cal. 3035/3135-type Microstella
89	  nuts: "allow setting over a range of 150 seconds per day"; low-head pair "one division of the graduated
90	  scale represent 1 seconds per day", high-head pair 2 s/day per division; "to set the watch on fast,
91	  turn the screw clockwise" (screw moves inward)
92	  (https://boley.de/downloads/48ba47cc7d854ba0ab446fdef4117350/Operating%20instructions.pdf).
93	  Omega 8xxx co-axial free-sprung screws: Type A "one complete revolution = 52 seconds", Type B
94	  "= 86 seconds" per day; German text gives 1 and 1.5 s/day per scale division, English says 1 for both
95	  (https://boley.de/downloads/0393584e7d0b443b967ab21ca75d98b9/Operating%20instructions.pdf).
96	  150 s/day full range implies ΔI/I = 0.35 %; 86 s/day per turn implies 0.2 % per turn.
97	- **[V] Vintage practice.** Fritts 1881, §346: compensation balances carry "four mean-time screws ...
98	  a quarter of a circle apart, and hence also termed quarter-screws"; §332: drawing the mean-time screws
99	  out "to cause a loss of a few seconds per day, (two to five, generally)". Timing washers under screws
100	  are the other inertia-only adjustment (Horopedia, https://horopedia.org/balance).
101	- **[P] Relative leverage.** SJX notes a change in r is more effective than the same change in L
102	  because r is squared in I = m·r². Correct for a single mass; for the whole rim I ∝ r².
103	
104	## Numbers to use in the simulation
105	
106	| Quantity | Value | Confidence |
107	|---|---|---|
108	| Period | T = 2π√(I/k); f = 1/T; bph = 7200·f | High [V] |
109	| Hairspring stiffness | k = E·h·t³/(12·L); expose k ∝ 1/L through L only | High on form, medium on 1/12 constant |
110	| Rate from length | rate(s/day) = −43200·ΔL/L (first order) | High [V], matches Horopedia 0.02 mm ≈ 10 s/day |
111	| Rate from inertia | rate(s/day) = −43200·ΔI/I | High [V] |
112	| Modern calibre (ETA 2824-2 style) | 28,800 A/h, 4 Hz, T = 0.25 s, lift angle 50°, I = 1.2×10⁻⁹ kg·m², k = 7.6×10⁻⁷ N·m/rad, L = 100 mm | Beat rate and lift angle high; I medium-high (patent); k derived |
113	| Vintage calibre | 18,000 A/h, 2.5 Hz, T = 0.4 s; pick I in 1.5–3×10⁻⁹ kg·m² and derive k | Beat rate high; I is a design choice [X] |
114	| Regulator index gain | ΔL per degree = r_outer·π/180 with r_outer = 4.5 mm → ≈ 0.08 mm/deg ≈ 34 s/day per degree at L = 100 mm | Medium-low, derived; forum data 40–50 s/day per 0.1 mm agrees |
115	| Regulator puzzle ("gains about 40 s/day") | index ≈ 1.2° toward F, or ΔL/L ≈ −0.09 % | Medium, follows from the above |
116	| Timing screws | 1–2 s/day per scale division, 50–150 s/day full range, inward = fast, move pairs together | High for Rolex/Omega (manufacturer tool manuals); medium that it transfers to other calibres |
117	| Sensitivity sanity check | 1 s/day = 2.3×10⁻⁵ fractional change in L, I or k | High [V] |
118	# Beat rates and how a timegrapher reads a movement
119	
120	Research note for The Watchmaker's Bench, 2026-11-01. Sources read directly: the `tg` open-source timegrapher source (vacaboja), Witschi product leaflets and the WisioScope product page, ETA's CT 2824-2 technical communication, Ciechanowski's *Mechanical Watch*, Wikipedia (ETA SA, Lever escapement), Caliber Corner, Watchguy's lift-angle table, and WatchRepairTalk threads. Claims are tagged **[verified]** (read in a primary or owning source), **[secondary]** (plausible, only seen second-hand), or **[unverified]**.
121	
122	## (a) Beat rates, beat period, balance frequency
123	
124	One **beat** (also "vibration", "alternance", French *alternance*, hence ETA's "A/h" or "alt/h") is one half-swing of the balance, from one extreme to the other. Each half-swing releases one escape-wheel tooth and makes one tick. One full oscillation is two beats. **[verified]** Ciechanowski: "the balance wheel does a full back-and-forth swing four times per second, hitting the pallet fork twice during each cycle, for a total of 8 beats per second or 28,800 beats per hour." ETA's CT 2824-2 lists "Fréquence 28'800 alt/h" and "Typical angle lift of balance 50°".
125	
126	| bph | beat period (s) | oscillation period T (s) | balance frequency (Hz) | beats per day |
127	|---|---|---|---|---|
128	| 18,000 | 0.2000 | 0.4000 | 2.5 | 432,000 |
129	| 19,800 | 0.1818 | 0.3636 | 2.75 | 475,200 |
130	| 21,600 | 0.1667 | 0.3333 | 3.0 | 518,400 |
131	| 25,200 | 0.1429 | 0.2857 | 3.5 | 604,800 |
132	| 28,800 | 0.1250 | 0.2500 | 4.0 | 691,200 |
133	| 36,000 | 0.1000 | 0.2000 | 5.0 | 864,000 |
134	
135	Formulas: beat period = 3600 / bph; T = 7200 / bph; f = bph / 7200. **[verified]** by arithmetic and matched to `tg` (`compute_period` searches around `7200 * sample_rate / bph`, so `tg`'s internal "period" is the full oscillation, two beats). `tg` presets exactly this list plus 12,000, 14,400, 17,280, 43,200 and 72,000 bph; Witschi instruments accept 3,600 to 72,000 A/h. **[verified]**
136	
137	## (b) How the timegrapher derives rate, beat error and amplitude
138	
139	**Rate.** The machine measures the actual tick-to-tick interval against the nominal one for the selected beat rate and scales the fractional error to a day. In `tg` (`computer.c`): `rate = (7200 / (bph * T_measured) - 1) * 24 * 3600` s/day, where `T_measured` is the measured two-beat period in seconds. Equivalent: rate = (T_nominal / T_measured − 1) × 86,400. Positive means the watch runs fast. **[verified, tg source]** The sensitivity is tiny per beat: 10 s/day at 28,800 bph is 14.5 µs per beat, so machines average many beats before displaying. Witschi quotes ±0.1 s/d accuracy with ranges of ±999 s/d. **[verified, Witschi X1 leaflet]** The lift angle setting does not affect rate. **[verified, tg source; secondary on forums]**
140	
141	**Beat error.** With a beat error the tick→tock interval d1 and tock→tick interval d2 are unequal. `tg` computes `be = T/2 - d1` (`algo.c` `compute_parameters`), reported as |be| in ms. Since d2 = T − d1, this equals |d2 − d1| / 2, which is also exactly the horizontal separation of the two trace lines. **[verified, tg source]** Whether Witschi and Weishi report the half-difference (trace separation) or the full difference |d2 − d1| I could not confirm from a Witschi manual; forum and vendor guides only say "the difference between tic and toc". **[unverified; see recommendation below]** Range on every machine is 0 to 9.9 ms, resolution 0.1 ms. **[verified, Witschi leaflets; Weishi manual via search snippet, secondary]**
142	
143	**Amplitude.** Acoustic machines cannot see the balance, so they time how long the balance takes to cross the lift angle, the arc over which the impulse pin is engaged with the pallet fork. Witschi's explanation, quoted on WatchRepairTalk: "To calculate the amplitude, the time between the first pulse and the third pulse of the beat noise is measured. Between these two pulses, the balance wheel rotates a certain angle. This so-called lift angle is determined by the construction of the movement and is entered as a parameter. The larger the amplitude ... the shorter is the time it needs to traverse this angle." **[secondary, forum quote attributed to Witschi]** Witschi's own WisioScope page confirms the principle by contrast: an optical sensor gives "actual amplitude, independent of lift angle". **[verified]**
144	
145	The formula, from simple harmonic motion θ(t) = A·sin(2πt/T) with the lift angle λ centred on the rest position, is:
146	
147	    A = (λ / 2) / sin(π · Δt / T)
148	
149	where Δt is the unlock-to-lock interval within one beat and T is the full oscillation period (two beats). This is exactly what `tg` implements: `amp = la * 0.5 / sin(M_PI * pulse / period)` (`algo.c` `compute_amplitude`), and the inverse `asin(lift_angle / (2 * amp)) / M_PI` in `output_panel.c`. `tg` only accepts a result if both tick and tock give 135° to 360° and agree within 60°. **[verified, tg source]** The formula in the task brief, `lift_angle / (2π·Δt/T)`, is the small-angle approximation of this and is wrong by a few percent at normal amplitudes; use the sine form. Worked values at λ = 52°: 28,800 bph, A = 280° gives Δt = 7.4 ms; A = 200° gives 10.4 ms; 18,000 bph, A = 280° gives 11.8 ms. The reported amplitude is the half-amplitude: the swing from the rest position to one extreme, so "280°" means 280° each way. **[secondary, Watchguy comment; consistent with the formula]**
150	
151	**Why 52°.** It is the long-standing default on timing machines (`tg` `DEFAULT_LA 52`; the Weishi 1000 manual says "factory set it to 52°", range 30° to 70°; Caliber Corner: "52° is a generally assumed average and also the default lift angle on most timing machines", most calibres fall "between 48-54 degrees"). **[verified for tg; secondary for Weishi and the "why"]** Real values differ by calibre. ETA states 50° for the 2824-2. **[verified, ETA CT 2824-2, 2011 and 2022 editions]** Watchguy's table lists ETA 2824 53°, 2892-A2 52°, 7750 49°, 6497 44°, Seiko 7S26/4R36 53°, Rolex 3135 52°, Unitas 52°. **[secondary, community table]** Amplitude reads linearly in λ, so a 1° error in the setting is about a 2% error in amplitude. Caliber Corner's example (52° vs 51° taking a reading from 239° to 228°) is larger than that and I could not reconcile it. **[unverified]** Witschi machines accept 10° to 90°. **[verified]**
152	
153	## (c) What the trace shows
154	
155	Each tick is plotted as one dot. The horizontal position (on a vertical strip like `tg`'s, or the vertical position on the horizontal Witschi/Weishi display) is the tick's time offset measured modulo the nominal beat period; successive beats advance by one row. If the watch runs exactly on time every dot lands in the same column. If it runs fast, each tick arrives slightly early and the dots drift, so the line's slope is the rate. In `tg`: `slope = -rate * zoom / 86400` in units of strip width per beat, with strip width = beat period / 10 (12.5 ms at 28,800 bph, 20 ms at 18,000), and a horizontal guide line every 10 s. **[verified, tg `output_panel.c`, `PAPERSTRIP_ZOOM 10`]** Ticks and tocks alternate, so with beat error the odd and even dots form two parallel lines separated by the beat error in ms; a single clean line means near-zero beat error. **[verified in tg; secondary for Witschi/Weishi]** Witschi's Watch Expert III leaflet gives the display scale as "Time scale adjustable from 1 up to 9 mm / ms (zoom)" on a 256 × 64-dot screen, and the Weishi 1900 display is 480 dots wide; so one screen is a few hundred beats, roughly 10 to 60 s of ticking. **[verified for Witschi; secondary for Weishi]** Scatter in the dots means an unstable escapement; two lines with different slopes do not occur in a healthy movement.
156	
157	## (d) The sounds of one Swiss lever beat
158	
159	Witschi's amplitude method implies three audible pulses per beat: (1) **unlocking**, the impulse pin hits the fork and the pallet stone slides off the escape-wheel tooth against the draw; (2) **impulse**, the tooth slides down the pallet's impulse plane and pushes the balance; (3) **drop/lock**, the escape wheel drops and the next tooth lands on the locking face of the other pallet while the lever hits the banking pin. The WatchRepairTalk quote attributes the measured pulses to "the escape-wheel tooth meeting the locking plane of the pallet-stone and the lever hitting the banking-pin". **[secondary]** The lever escapement phases themselves (unlock, impulse, drop, lock, with draw holding the lever on the banking) are standard. **[verified, Wikipedia Lever escapement; Ciechanowski's step list "escape wheel unlocks ... pallet fork pushes the jewel roller ... escape wheel locks again"]** Timing: pulse 1 to pulse 3 is the lift-angle traverse, Δt in the formula above, so about 7 to 12 ms at 280° depending on beat rate, and longer at lower amplitude. `tg` searches for pulse 1 up to one eighth of a period (31 ms at 28,800 bph) before the loudest pulse and treats the loudest pulse as the lock. **[verified, tg source]** The relative loudness and the position of the impulse pulse between the two I could not verify from a primary source. **[unverified]**
160	
161	## (e) Tolerances
162	
163	- ETA 2824-2 grades, mean rate and max positional variation: Standard, 2 positions, ±12 s/d, variation ±30; Elaboré, 3 positions, ±7 s/d, variation ±20; Top, 5 positions, ±4 s/d, variation ±15; Chronometer follows COSC (−4/+6 s/d mean daily rate). **[secondary, Wikipedia ETA SA; ETA's own manufacturing-information sheet with amplitude and beat-error limits was not found online]**
164	- Beat error: vendor and watchmaker guides treat under about 0.5 to 0.6 ms as good; ETA's own figure not found. Forum readings on a freshly serviced 2824-2 show 0.1 ms. **[secondary]**
165	- Amplitude: Caliber Corner quotes 260° to 310° for a healthy movement at full wind, dial up, falling as oils age; forum readings on a serviced 2824-2 show 278° to 286°. Vertical positions read lower than dial up. **[secondary]** Machines refuse readings below 70° to 80° (Witschi) or 135° (`tg`). **[verified]**
166	- Measurement precision of the instruments: rate ±0.1 s/d, amplitude ±0.4° to ±1°, beat error ±0.1 ms. **[verified, Witschi leaflets]**
167	
168	## Numbers and formulas to use in the simulation
169	
170	| Item | Recommendation | Confidence |
171	|---|---|---|
172	| Beat definition | 1 beat = 1 half-swing = 1 tick; beat period = 3600/bph; T = 7200/bph | High (verified) |
173	| Default calibre beat rate | 28,800 bph (4 Hz), optional second calibre 18,000 bph (2.5 Hz) | High |
174	| Rate | `rate_s_per_day = (T_nominal / T_measured - 1) * 86400`, average over many beats; + = fast | High (tg source) |
175	| Beat error | Display `abs(d2 - d1) / 2` in ms (equals the trace-line separation, matches tg); note in GLOSSARY that some machines may show the full difference | Medium (tg verified; Witschi convention unverified) |
176	| Amplitude | `A = (lift / 2) / sin(pi * dt / T)` where dt = unlock-to-lock time; invert to produce dt from the simulated amplitude | High (tg source, SHM derivation) |
177	| Lift angle | Parameter per calibre; machine default 52°, sim calibre 50° for an ETA 2824-2-like movement, 44° for a 6497-like pocket calibre | High for 52° default and ETA 50°; Medium for others |
178	| Healthy amplitude | 270° to 300° dial up at full wind; below 200° is a fault; trace invalid below 135° | Medium (secondary only) |
179	| Healthy rate / beat error | Within ±10 s/d and under 0.5 ms as "healthy"; ±12 s/d ETA Standard; puzzle "runs fast" at +40 s/d is clearly out of spec | Medium |
180	| Trace geometry | One dot per beat, x = tick offset mod beat period, slope ∝ rate, two lines separated by beat error; show about 300 beats per screen (about 37 s at 28,800 bph) | High for the mechanism; Medium for the screen scale |
181	| Beat sounds | Three pulses per beat: unlock, impulse, lock; pulse 1 to pulse 3 spans the lift angle (7 to 12 ms at 280°) | Medium (Witschi description is second-hand) |
182	
183	Sources: `tg` source files `algo.c`, `computer.c`, `output_panel.c`, `tg.h` at https://github.com/vacaboja/tg ; Witschi Watch Expert III leaflet (cousinsuk.com/PDF/skus/643_leaflet_watchexpertIII t20214.pdf), Chronoscope X1 leaflet (cousinsuk.com/PDF/skus/3531_T32439_leaflet_chronoscope-X1 (G2).pdf), WisioScope page https://www.witschi.com/en/?p=2757 ; ETA CT 2824-2 https://shopb2b.eta.ch/technicaldocuments/index/pdf/id/1883 and /1884 ; https://ciechanow.ski/mechanical-watch/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ETA_SA ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lever_escapement ; https://calibercorner.com/lift-angle/ ; https://calibercorner.com/amplitude/ ; https://watchguy.co.uk/cgi-bin/lift_angles ; https://watchguy.co.uk/?p=2502 ; https://www.watchrepairtalk.com/topic/2727-how-does-the-timegrapheror-vibrograph-measure-amplitude/ ; Weishi 1000 manual (manuals.online, via search snippet only).
184	# 03 — Balance amplitude and isochronism
185	
186	Research note for The Watchmaker's Bench. Date: 2026-11-01. Scope: (a) how amplitude follows mainspring torque, (b) why amplitude changes rate in a Swiss lever watch and in which direction, (c) other isochronism effects (hairspring, regulator pins, overcoil, knocking), (d) an analytic model to encode. Each claim is tagged **[V]** verified from a primary source, **[P]** plausible but secondary/forum only, or **[X]** could not verify.
187	
188	## Sources actually read
189	
190	- Airy, G. B., "On the Disturbances of Pendulums and Balances, and on the Theory of Escapements", Trans. Cambridge Phil. Soc. III (read 1826, printed 1830). Transcription: https://theindex.nawcc.org/Articles/AiryOnPendulumsAndBalanceWheels.htm ; annotated PDF by D. Roegel: https://members.loria.fr/Roegel/loc/airy1827annotated.pdf
191	- Hoyng, P., "Dynamics and performance of clock pendulums", arXiv:1501.03673 (2015). https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1501.03673
192	- Witschi Electronic AG, "Testing methods for mechanical watches" (2025 PDF). https://www.witschi.com/wp-content/uploads/firmwares/o0kUcAHH/20250717_witschi_testing-methods-for-mechanical-watches_en.pdf
193	- US patent 9,323,223 B2 (balance-and-hairspring movement with improved isochronism). https://patents.google.com/patent/US9323223B2/en
194	- Horopedia (Swiss watchmaking-schools encyclopedia), "Amplitude". https://horopedia.org/amplitude/
195	- Watches by SJX, "In-Depth: Understanding Isochronism and Oscillators" (Dec 2025). https://watchesbysjx.com/2025/12/in-depth-isochronism.html ; and "Insight: The Overcoil Hairspring, From Breguet to Phillips". https://watchesbysjx.com/2025/06/overcoil-hairspring-explained.html
196	- WatchTime, Brunner, "Throwing a Curve: ... Mainsprings". https://www.watchtime.com/brands/tourbillon-watches/throwing-a-curve-the-how-what-when-where-and-why-of-mainsprings
197	- Stoimenov et al., "Lever watch escapements", FME Transactions 40 (2012). https://simlab.mas.bg.ac.rs/_media/istrazivanje/fme/vol40/1/03_mstoimenov.pdf
198	- Wikipedia "Mainspring", "Balance spring" (for Phillips 1861 and the torque-curve figures). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainspring
199	- Forum threads (practising watchmakers, treated as [P]): Watch Repair Talk "Isochronism: how is it adjusted in practice?" https://www.watchrepairtalk.com/topic/20711-isochronism-how-is-it-adjusted-in-practice/ ; "Troubleshooting Isochronism" https://www.watchrepairtalk.com/topic/36668-troubleshooting-isochronism/ ; "Mainspring strength" https://www.watchrepairtalk.com/topic/6853-mainspring-strength/ ; "mapping mainspring torque and fusees" https://www.watchrepairtalk.com/topic/15114-mapping-mainspring-torque-and-fusees/ ; Omega Forums "Watchmaking with the BHI" p.5 https://omegaforums.net/threads/watchmaking-with-the-bhi.39076/page-5
200	- Not reachable: Minnix 1968 "Mathematical Model of the Detached Lever Escapement" (DTIC AD0685882, site under maintenance); Ciechanowski's *Mechanical Watch* was read but contains no amplitude, torque-curve or isochronism numbers, only qualitative statements that the train reduces torque at the escape wheel and that oil reduces losses. Daniels *Watchmaking* and de Carle were not available online; nothing below is attributed to them.
201	
202	## (a) Amplitude versus mainspring torque
203	
204	- **Torque curve shape.** [V] A going-barrel mainspring gives strongest torque at full wind, a relatively flat middle range, and a steep fall near exhaustion (WatchTime; Wikipedia "Mainspring" torque-curve figures). The last few turns are "ineffective turns" whose force drops off sharply and are not counted on (vintagewatchstraps.com mainspring page, quoting Britten) [P].
205	- **How much it falls in 24 h.** [P, industry rule of thumb] "Torque arriving at the escape wheel should decline by no more than 15 percent the first day" (WatchTime/Brunner). A typical wristwatch barrel makes ~6 turns of wind for ~40–44 h, ~7.5 h per barrel turn (nickelsilver, WRT fusee thread) [P]. Winding and unwinding branches form a hysteresis loop (US 8,356,930 abstract, seen via search only) [P]. No measured N·mm-vs-hours dataset for a modern wristwatch calibre was found [X].
206	- **Energy balance per beat.** [V] In Hoyng's averaged equations the oscillator energy is λ²/2 and linear (viscous) damping removes energy at rate ∝ λ² (his Eq. 9: dλ/dt = −ελ + ∮m cosψ dψ). The escapement's energy input per period balances this at steady state, giving amplitude ∝ √(driving torque) for a constant-torque escapement (Eq. 19) and λ = (e/2πε)^½ for a single impulse of energy e (App. C). [P] SJX cites Conus's thesis that viscous pivot friction dominates damping of a lubricated sprung balance, which supports losses ∝ A². With Coulomb (dry) friction instead, losses ∝ A and A ∝ torque. Real watches sit between the two.
207	- **Typical amplitude values.** [V] Witschi: "In most modern mechanical movements, the amplitude typically ranges between 270° and 310° when fully wound"; lift angle "approximately 51°"; amplitude A = λ / (2 sin(πft)) from lift time t. [V] Horopedia: amplitude "decreases as this energy diminishes"; construction limits it to "maximum 280°–300° depending on the lift angle". [P] Service-bench norms: 275–280° full wind and >225° at 24 h (WRT "Mainspring strength"); BHI teaching material quoted as 270° typical / 310° max at full wind, minimum 200° at 24 h; an ETA 2892 "only drops 10% maximum at 24H"; a 1950s 30 mm Omega shows "perhaps a 40 degree drop" at 24 h (nickelsilver). Witschi's own worked example drops 288°→278° mean (vertical 284°→272°) between 0 h and 24 h.
208	- **Verdict on the brief's 280°→200°.** A healthy modern movement drops ~10–15% (280°→~240–250°) in 24 h. 280°→200° (−29%) is a tired-spring or dirty-train watch, which is fine for the "afternoon slump" puzzle but should not be the healthy default.
209	
210	## (b) Why amplitude changes rate in a lever escapement, and the sign
211	
212	- **Airy's theorem.** [V] Airy, Ex. 7–8: an impulse given exactly at the lowest point (balance at rest position, zero crossing) leaves the period unchanged; a force acting "before reaching the lowest point tends to diminish the time of oscillation, and that after it to increase the time". So: impulse before mid-swing → gain; after mid-swing → loss. He states explicitly that because the hairspring torque is proportional to angle, "the same equations which apply to the motion of a pendulum will apply also to the motion of a balance", and that Mudge's lever "possess[es] almost exactly the same properties as the dead-beat escapement", whose rate effect "may be made as small as we please" but "cannot, however, be made absolutely nothing".
213	- **Modern form.** [V] Hoyng Eq. 10: rate − 1 = −λ²/16 − (1/λ)∮ m sinψ dψ; the second term "is called the escapement error ... as computed already by Airy". For a single impulse of energy e at phase ψ₁ (Eq. 29–30): escapement error = −(e / 2πλ²)·tan ψ₁, which "either increases the rate (ψ₁ < 0, impulse before a zero), or reduces it (ψ₁ > 0, impulse after a zero)". Note the 1/λ² and tan ψ₁ = φ₁/√(λ²−φ₁²): a fixed impulse angle φ₁ matters more as amplitude λ shrinks.
214	- **Applied to the Swiss lever.** [V] US 9,323,223 (industry patent): the oscillator "is subjected to a resistant torque before the line of centres, and this causes a loss"; then "a drive torque firstly before the line of centres, which causes a gain, then after the line of centres, which causes a loss"; "the escapement thus produces a rate loss and this disturbance caused by the escapement is greater for small oscillation amplitudes". SJX (Dec 2025) gives the same phase-by-phase account: unlocking → loss; impulse before equilibrium → gain; impulse after equilibrium and the run to banking → loss; net loss. Stoimenov: the lever engages over about ±15° of a ±270° swing, so the balance is free for >88% of the period [V].
215	- **So which way does a real watch go?** The *escapement alone* makes a Swiss lever watch **lose more as amplitude falls** [V, three independent sources]. But bench experience often shows the opposite net sign: "the movement works faster in the end of power reserve, when the amplitude is smaller" (nevenbekriev), "if the rate is higher when the amplitude is lower ... check the hairspring is centred in the regulator pins" (Klassiker), "at very low amplitudes the rate can increase considerably" [P]. The gain comes from the hairspring/regulator-pin system (section c), which is deliberately set to over-compensate the escapement loss. The patent quantifies the compensation designers aim for: a hairspring-induced gain "of at least 2 s/d, or at least 4 s/d, or even at least 6 s/d, or even at least 8 s/d, at an amplitude of 150° with respect to an amplitude of 300°" [V]. Witschi's worked example (0 h vs 24 h) shows gains of +1.7 and +2.9 s/d where amplitude fell 8° and 23° and essentially no change where amplitude did not fall [V, but an illustrative dataset].
216	- **Magnitude.** [P] Escapement-only loss: order 2–8 s/d over a 150° amplitude drop, i.e. roughly 0.1–0.5 s/d per 10°, growing as amplitude falls. Net, pin-compensated watch: typically ±1 s/d per 10° over the 240–300° band (Witschi example, Ie values of a few s/d). Pathological pin contact: −53 → −19.3 s/d as amplitude fell 249° → 204° (Seiko Marvel case, ≈ +7 s/d per 10°) [P]. No source gives a single universal coefficient [X].
217	
218	## (c) Other isochronism effects
219	
220	- **Regulator pins (flat spring).** [P, consistent across watchmakers] With the spring centred and a correct gap, at very low amplitude the spring is free between the pins (full length → slow), at higher amplitude it touches the pins more (shorter effective length → faster), averaging out over the normal band (JohnR725). If the spring rests against one pin, the watch "runs fast at low amplitudes" and slows as amplitude lifts it off (JohnR725, nevenbekriev). Opening the gap "will slow the rate, more so for low amplitudes" (Klassiker). Witschi lists "clearance in the regulator pins" among the main isochronism factors [V]. US 7,648,265 (via search): "depending on the distance of the regulator pins, oscillations at small amplitudes can be speeded up or slowed down" [P].
221	- **Pinning point / stud, Breguet overcoil.** [V] A flat spring with a fixed outer pinning point cannot "breathe" concentrically; the eccentric development loads the pivots and disturbs isochronism (SJX overcoil article; Wikipedia citing Phillips 1861, who proved a spring whose centre of gravity stays on the balance axis is isochronous). The overcoil raises the last coil and curves it toward the pinning point so the body develops concentrically; Phillips' conditions fix the end-curve's centre of gravity. [P] With an overcoil, "the overcoil is calculated to be isochronous"; residual error is corrected by reshaping it: closer to the balance centre raises the rate at low amplitude, further out lowers it (nickelsilver). Overcoil watches also need a pin-free or wide-pin regulator, which is why they hold rate 0 h→24 h despite a 40° drop (nickelsilver, same post).
222	- **Hairspring quality / material.** [P] Steel springs: centrifugal effect on balance arms slows the rate at high amplitude while less pin contact raises it, partly compensating (nickelsilver). Modern Nivarox-class alloys remove most of this.
223	- **Knocking / rebanking at very high amplitude.** [V] Horopedia: beyond ~280–300° (lift-angle dependent) "a knock (rebate) phenomenon causes the oscillator to run away and results in an exaggerated advance". [P] Mechanism: the impulse pin strikes the outside of the fork horn (the lever is against its banking pin) and bounces back early, truncating the swing → shorter period → sudden large gain, with a "galloping" sound; timegrapher traces go chaotic and reported amplitude becomes meaningless. Thresholds quoted: ~320–330° at full wind for a modern 51–52° lift-angle calibre; Omega guidance quoted as <315° dial-up automatic, <325° manual; a Raketa case shows disorder "as soon as the amplitude reaches near 325 degrees"; overbanking (pin stuck behind the horn) needs ~350°. Causes: too strong a mainspring, fresh lubrication, dial-up position [P].
224	
225	## (d) Analytic model used in the literature
226	
227	[V] Airy (1826) / Hoyng (2015) averaged (KBM) equations, per oscillation: dλ/dt = −ελ + ∮ m cosψ dψ (amplitude); rate − 1 = −(1/λ)∮ m sinψ dψ (escapement error; the −λ²/16 circular-error term is a pendulum term and is absent for a Hooke's-law hairspring). Sign rule: impulse before the zero crossing → gain, after → loss; magnitude ∝ (impulse energy / oscillator energy) × tan(impulse phase). Single impulse of energy e at angle φ₁: Δrate = −(e/2πλ²)·φ₁/√(λ²−φ₁²). Everything below is this model plus an empirical hairspring term.
228	
229	## Numbers and model to use in the simulation
230	
231	| Quantity | Recommendation | Confidence / source |
232	|---|---|---|
233	| Mainspring torque T(t), t in hours, healthy manual calibre | T/T₀ = 1 − 0.15·(t/24) for 0 ≤ t ≤ 36 h (linear, −15 % in 24 h); then fall linearly to 0 at t ≈ 42 h ("ineffective turns"); stop when amplitude < ~120° | Medium: WatchTime 15 %/day rule; ~6 turns × 7.5 h/turn; Britten via vintagewatchstraps |
234	| Amplitude from torque | A = A₀·(T/T₀)^k, k = 0.7 (between viscous k=0.5 and Coulomb k=1); A₀ = 280° dial-up, 260° vertical | Medium for the law (Hoyng Eq. 19, App. C); low for k |
235	| Amplitude curve, healthy watch | 0 h 280°, 12 h 265°, 24 h 250°, 36 h 235°, 40 h ~190°, stops ≈ 42 h | Medium: Witschi 270–310° full wind; bench 10–15 % drop at 24 h |
236	| Amplitude curve, "afternoon slump" puzzle (tired/thin spring or dirty train) | use T/T₀ = 1 − 0.40·(t/24): 280° → ~200° at 24 h | Medium: brief's figure matches BHI "minimum 200° at 24 h" and WRT ">225° healthy" |
237	| Escapement error (always a loss, grows at low amplitude) | r_esc(A) = −k_e·(A_ref/A − 1), A_ref = 280°, k_e ≈ 8 s/d (gives −1.1 s/d at 250°, −3.7 at 200°, −6.9 at 150°) | Sign: high (Airy, Hoyng, patent, SJX). Magnitude: low–medium (patent's 2–8 s/d over 300°→150°) |

240	| Knocking threshold | if A > 330° (dial-up) clip the swing at 330° and add a gain of order +50 to +300 s/d with a noisy trace; show amplitude as unreliable | Medium for threshold (320–330° quoted widely, Horopedia 280–300° for older geometry); low for the gain figure |
241	| Lift angle for timegrapher amplitude | 51° (Witschi "approximately 51°"), 52° also common; lever engaged ≈ ±15° of swing (Stoimenov) | High |
242	| Amplitude reading formula | A = λ / (2·sin(π·f·t_lift)), f in Hz, t_lift in s | High (Witschi Eq. 6) |
